questions.question: A healthcare company is building a system to predict whether patients will develop diabetes within five years. The team has 100,000 historical records with lab results, demographics, lifestyle factors, and a binary outcome column. Which machine learning approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Reinforcement learning with reward-based feedback

explanation.summary: Reinforcement learning optimizes actions through rewards rather than predicting labeled outcomes.
explanation.why: Reinforcement learning is designed for environments where an agent learns through rewards and penalties over time. This healthcare problem already contains labeled historical outcomes indicating whether diabetes developed, making it a supervised classification problem instead of a sequential decision-making task.
explanation.comparison: Reinforcement learning focuses on action policies, whereas classification predicts labels from historical examples.

options.text: Unsupervised learning using clustering algorithms

explanation.summary: Clustering discovers hidden groups without using labeled outcomes.
explanation.why: Unsupervised learning is useful when no target labels exist and the goal is to discover patterns or groupings. In this case, the dataset already includes a binary outcome indicating whether patients developed diabetes, so supervised learning is the correct approach.
explanation.keyDistinction: The presence of labeled outcomes makes this supervised learning.

options.text: Supervised learning using a classification algorithm

explanation.summary: Classification algorithms predict labeled categorical outcomes from historical data.
explanation.why: The dataset contains historical records with a binary target outcome indicating whether diabetes developed. This makes the problem a supervised binary classification task where the model learns patterns from labeled examples to predict future outcomes.

options.text: Generative AI with a large language model

explanation.summary: Large language models are optimized for generative tasks rather than structured binary prediction.
explanation.why: Generative AI models are commonly used for generating text, summarization, and conversational tasks. Predicting whether a patient will develop diabetes from structured historical records is better solved using supervised classification techniques.
explanation.comparison: Generative AI creates content, while classification predicts categories.

questions.question: A bank's fraud detection model flags fraudulent credit card transactions with 99.2% accuracy. However, only 0.3% of historical transactions are actually fraudulent. Why is accuracy misleading here, and which evaluation approach better reflects effectiveness?

options.text: Accuracy is invalid for binary classification and cannot be used at all

explanation.summary: Accuracy can still be used in binary classification but may become misleading with imbalanced data.
explanation.why: Accuracy is a valid metric for binary classification tasks, but it becomes unreliable when one class heavily dominates the dataset. In fraud detection, the model may achieve high accuracy while failing to detect actual fraudulent transactions.

options.text: The model may be predicting all transactions as legitimate and still achieving high accuracy due to severe class imbalance

explanation.summary: Class imbalance can produce deceptively high accuracy while missing rare fraud cases.
explanation.why: Because only 0.3% of transactions are fraudulent, a model could predict every transaction as legitimate and still achieve extremely high accuracy. Metrics such as precision, recall, F1-score, and PR-AUC better evaluate fraud detection performance because they focus on minority-class detection.
keyPoints: Recall is critical in fraud detection
explanation.comparison: Recall and precision provide better insight into fraud detection effectiveness than raw accuracy.

options.text: Accuracy only works for multi-class problems with three or more categories

explanation.summary: Accuracy applies to both binary and multi-class classification problems.
explanation.why: Accuracy measures the proportion of correct predictions and can be used for binary classification. The issue in this scenario is class imbalance rather than the number of categories.

options.text: The dataset is too small at 0.3% positives to evaluate any model reliably

explanation.summary: The problem is imbalance rather than dataset size alone.
explanation.why: A low percentage of fraud cases does not automatically make evaluation impossible. The key challenge is selecting metrics that properly measure performance on the minority class.

questions.question: A retail analytics company wants to discover natural groupings in its customer base without preconceived categories, using purchase frequency, order value, product categories, and shopping times. There are no predefined segments. Which approach lets the algorithm identify structure on its own?

options.text: Supervised classification using a Random Forest model

explanation.summary: Supervised classification requires predefined labels or categories.
explanation.why: Random Forest classification learns from labeled training data. Since the problem states there are no predefined customer segments, supervised learning is not appropriate.

options.text: Reinforcement learning with a reward function based on campaign response

explanation.summary: Reinforcement learning optimizes actions through rewards rather than discovering clusters.
explanation.why: Reinforcement learning is suitable for sequential decision-making tasks where an agent learns through rewards. Customer segmentation without labels is better addressed using clustering methods.

options.text: Linear regression to predict customer lifetime value

explanation.summary: Linear regression predicts numeric values rather than grouping similar customers.
explanation.why: Regression models estimate continuous outcomes such as revenue or lifetime value. The goal here is segmentation and pattern discovery, not numeric prediction.
explanation.comparison: Regression predicts quantities, while clustering discovers groups.

options.text: K-means clustering to discover natural customer segments

explanation.summary: K-means clustering identifies hidden groupings without labeled categories.
explanation.why: K-means is an unsupervised learning algorithm that groups similar data points together based on feature similarity. Since the company does not have predefined customer segments, clustering is the correct approach for discovering natural structure in the customer data.

questions.question: A logistics company's package delivery model has become less accurate over three months, even though the model is unchanged. Investigation shows traffic patterns, fuel costs, and delivery volumes have shifted significantly since training. What phenomenon is the team experiencing?

options.text: Data drift is occurring as real-world input data distributions shift over time

explanation.summary: Data drift occurs when production data changes from the original training distribution.
explanation.why: The model performance declined because real-world conditions such as traffic patterns and delivery volumes changed after training. This causes the input distribution seen during inference to differ from the original training data, reducing predictive accuracy over time.

options.text: The model is overfitting to its training data

explanation.summary: Overfitting occurs during training when a model memorizes training patterns too closely.
explanation.why: Overfitting is typically observed when training accuracy is much higher than validation or test accuracy from the beginning. This scenario specifically describes changing real-world conditions after deployment.

options.text: The model is underfitting due to insufficient complexity

explanation.summary: Underfitting happens when a model cannot capture underlying patterns during training.
explanation.why: Underfitting usually appears as poor performance on both training and test datasets from the start. The problem here emerged after environmental conditions changed over time.

options.text: Data leakage was present during the original training

explanation.summary: Data leakage involves unintended information contamination during training.
explanation.why: Data leakage causes unrealistically strong model performance during training or validation. It does not specifically explain gradual accuracy degradation caused by changing production conditions.

questions.question: A real estate technology company is building a model to predict housing prices in major metropolitan areas. The model will output a specific dollar amount as its prediction. The data science team needs to select appropriate evaluation metrics that work for this type of prediction.

options.text: Accuracy and F1 score

explanation.summary: Accuracy and F1-score are classification metrics rather than regression metrics.
explanation.why: These metrics evaluate categorical predictions such as fraud detection or sentiment classification. Housing price prediction outputs continuous numeric values, making regression metrics more appropriate.

options.text: Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) and Mean Absolute Error (MAE)

explanation.summary: RMSE and MAE measure prediction error for continuous numeric outputs.
explanation.why: Housing price prediction is a regression problem because the model outputs a specific dollar amount. MAE measures the average absolute prediction error, while RMSE penalizes large errors more heavily, making both valuable for evaluating regression performance.
explanation.comparison: RMSE penalizes large prediction errors more strongly than MAE.

options.text: AUC-ROC and Precision-Recall curve

explanation.summary: AUC-ROC and Precision-Recall evaluate classification model discrimination.
explanation.why: These metrics are commonly used for binary classification problems such as fraud detection. Predicting house prices is a regression task involving continuous values rather than class labels.

options.text: Confusion matrix and recall

explanation.summary: Confusion matrices and recall apply to categorical classification outcomes.
explanation.why: Recall measures the proportion of correctly identified positive cases in classification problems. Housing price prediction does not involve categorical outcomes and therefore requires regression-based metrics instead.

questions.question: A firm is comparing two credit risk models. Model A: 98% training accuracy, 67% test accuracy. Model B: 75% training accuracy, 73% test accuracy. What is happening with each model, and which is more suitable for production deployment?

options.text: Model A is the clear winner because its training accuracy is higher

explanation.summary: High training accuracy alone does not indicate good real-world generalization.
explanation.why: Model A performs extremely well on training data but poorly on test data, indicating overfitting. Production models should generalize well to unseen data rather than memorizing training examples.
explanation.comparison: Test performance is usually more important than training performance for deployment decisions.

options.text: Model A is overfitting; Model B generalizes better and is preferable

explanation.summary: Large train-test gaps indicate overfitting, while similar scores suggest better generalization.
explanation.why: Model A shows a major gap between training and test accuracy, meaning it memorized training data patterns without generalizing effectively. Model B has lower training accuracy but much closer training and test results, indicating stronger generalization to unseen data and better suitability for production.
explanation.comparison: Overfitting models often achieve very high training performance but weak test performance.

options.text: Both models are underfitting and need more complexity

explanation.summary: Underfitting occurs when a model performs poorly on both training and testing data.
explanation.why: Model A clearly achieves very high training accuracy, which contradicts underfitting. The issue is overfitting rather than insufficient model complexity.

options.text: Model B has data leakage because its train and test scores are similar

explanation.summary: Similar train and test scores usually indicate stable generalization rather than leakage.
explanation.why: Data leakage typically causes unrealistically high validation or test performance. Model B's similar scores instead suggest consistent behavior across datasets.

questions.question: A customer service team receives thousands of recorded calls daily and wants to automatically convert audio recordings into searchable written transcripts so supervisors can review interactions and analyze sentiment. Which AWS service performs this automatic speech recognition task?

options.text: Amazon Polly for text-to-speech synthesis

explanation.summary: Amazon Polly converts written text into spoken audio.
explanation.why: Polly is designed for text-to-speech generation, which is the reverse of the required speech-to-text functionality.
explanation.comparison: Polly performs text-to-speech, while Transcribe performs speech-to-text.

options.text: Amazon Translate for language conversion

explanation.summary: Amazon Translate converts text between languages rather than transcribing audio.
explanation.why: The requirement is automatic speech recognition from audio recordings, not multilingual translation.

options.text: Amazon Comprehend for natural language analysis

explanation.summary: Amazon Comprehend analyzes text but does not transcribe audio recordings.
explanation.why: Comprehend can perform sentiment analysis and entity extraction after text exists, but another service must first convert speech into text.

options.text: Amazon Transcribe for automatic speech recognition

explanation.summary: Amazon Transcribe converts spoken audio into searchable text transcripts.
explanation.why: Amazon Transcribe is AWS’s automatic speech recognition service that transforms audio recordings into written transcripts. It supports call center analytics, searchable conversations, speaker identification, timestamps, and downstream NLP analysis.

questions.question: A pharmaceutical firm needs to extract medication names, dosages, conditions, and procedures from millions of unstructured clinical notes. Compliance requires the service be specifically validated for medical and healthcare use. Which AWS service is the most appropriate choice?

options.text: Amazon Comprehend for general entity recognition

explanation.summary: General-purpose NLP lacks healthcare-specific medical specialization.
explanation.why: Amazon Comprehend performs generic natural language processing tasks but is not specifically designed or validated for healthcare terminology and medical entity extraction.

options.text: Amazon Textract to extract text from documents

explanation.summary: Textract extracts raw text but does not understand medical concepts.
explanation.why: Amazon Textract performs OCR and document text extraction. It cannot identify medical entities such as medications, conditions, dosages, or procedures semantically.
explanation.comparison: Textract extracts text structure, while Comprehend Medical extracts healthcare meaning.

options.text: Amazon Translate to standardize medical terminology

explanation.summary: Amazon Translate focuses on language translation rather than healthcare NLP.
explanation.why: The use case involves extracting medical entities from clinical notes, not translating languages between documents.

options.text: Amazon Comprehend Medical for healthcare-specific entity extraction

explanation.summary: Comprehend Medical extracts healthcare entities from unstructured clinical text.
explanation.why: Amazon Comprehend Medical is purpose-built for healthcare NLP workloads. It can identify medications, dosages, medical conditions, procedures, PHI, and clinical relationships from unstructured medical text while supporting healthcare-specific analysis requirements.

questions.question: A media streaming company wants personalized recommendations for 50 million subscribers based on viewing history, ratings, demographics, and content metadata. The company has no ML expertise and wants a fully managed AWS service handling the entire recommendation workflow. Which service fits?

options.text: Amazon Rekognition for content tagging

explanation.summary: Amazon Rekognition focuses on image and video analysis rather than recommendations.
explanation.why: Rekognition detects objects, labels, and faces in images or videos. It is not designed for personalized recommendation systems.

options.text: Amazon Forecast for time-series prediction

explanation.summary: Amazon Forecast specializes in demand and time-series forecasting.
explanation.why: Forecast predicts future numeric trends such as sales or inventory demand, not personalized content recommendations.

options.text: Amazon Personalize for managed real-time recommendations

explanation.summary: Amazon Personalize provides managed recommendation systems without deep ML expertise.
explanation.why: Amazon Personalize is a fully managed recommendation service that builds real-time personalization models using user interactions, metadata, and behavioral patterns. It is designed for recommendation use cases such as streaming content suggestions and personalized rankings.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker for custom model development

explanation.summary: SageMaker supports custom ML development but requires more ML expertise.
explanation.why: Although SageMaker can build recommendation systems, the question specifically asks for a fully managed recommendation workflow suitable for teams without ML specialists.
explanation.comparison: Personalize abstracts recommendation workflows, whereas SageMaker is a broader ML platform.

questions.question: A wildlife conservation group processes images from remote camera traps. The app must detect animal species, count individuals, and flag rare or endangered sightings. They need a managed service supporting custom labels plus pre-built object detection. Which capabilities should they use?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker only, building a CNN from scratch

explanation.summary: Building custom CNNs from scratch adds unnecessary complexity for managed image analysis needs.
explanation.why: While SageMaker can train custom computer vision models, the requirement specifically calls for a managed service with pre-built object detection and customizable labels.

options.text: Amazon Rekognition Image with Custom Labels for species-specific training

explanation.summary: Rekognition Custom Labels combines managed object detection with custom image classification.
explanation.why: Amazon Rekognition provides pre-trained image analysis capabilities such as object detection and labeling, while Custom Labels enables teams to train models for specialized wildlife species recognition without building deep learning infrastructure from scratch.

options.text: Amazon Textract for image processing

explanation.summary: Textract focuses on OCR and document text extraction rather than visual object recognition.
explanation.why: Textract is designed for extracting text from scanned documents and forms, not detecting animals or classifying wildlife imagery.

options.text: Amazon Comprehend for visual analysis

explanation.summary: Comprehend analyzes text rather than image content.
explanation.why: Amazon Comprehend is an NLP service for processing written language and cannot perform image-based species recognition tasks.

questions.question: A data science team plans to split its dataset into three subsets: one for actual learning, one for hyperparameter tuning and overfitting detection during development, and one reserved exclusively for a final unbiased performance estimate. Which split correctly maps to these three purposes?

options.text: Training set, validation set, test set

explanation.summary: Training, validation, and test datasets serve distinct stages of model development and evaluation.
explanation.why: The training set is used for model learning and parameter fitting. The validation set supports hyperparameter tuning, model selection, and overfitting detection during development. The test set remains untouched until final evaluation to provide an unbiased estimate of real-world model performance.

options.text: Test set, training set, validation set

explanation.summary: This ordering assigns incorrect roles to the datasets.
explanation.why: The test set should not be used before training or validation because it must remain isolated for final unbiased evaluation after development is complete.

options.text: Validation set, test set, training set

explanation.summary: Validation and testing datasets cannot replace the training dataset role.
explanation.why: The training dataset must be the primary dataset used for model learning. Validation and test datasets are intended for evaluation and tuning rather than direct training.
explanation.comparison: Training builds the model, while validation and testing evaluate it.

options.text: Production set, sandbox set, archive set

explanation.summary: These are not standard machine learning dataset split categories.
explanation.why: Machine learning workflows conventionally use training, validation, and test datasets to support learning, tuning, and final evaluation tasks.

questions.question: A startup wants to add machine learning but lacks data science staff. The team needs to build a customer churn model from tabular data in Amazon S3, and prefers a no-code or low-code visual interface with automatic data prep and one-click deployment. Which AWS service best fits?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Studio with Python notebooks

explanation.summary: SageMaker Studio is a coding-oriented ML development environment.
explanation.why: SageMaker Studio provides notebooks and advanced ML tooling intended for developers and data scientists. The scenario specifically requests no-code or low-code workflows suitable for non-experts.

options.text: Amazon EMR with Apache Spark MLlib

explanation.summary: EMR and Spark MLlib require significant engineering and ML expertise.
explanation.why: Amazon EMR is a big data analytics platform commonly used by experienced engineers and data scientists. It does not provide the no-code visual workflow requested.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Canvas for no-code ML

explanation.summary: SageMaker Canvas enables no-code machine learning workflows for business users.
explanation.why: Amazon SageMaker Canvas provides a visual interface for building ML models without writing code. It supports automatic data preparation, integration with Amazon S3, prediction workflows, and simplified deployment, making it ideal for teams without dedicated ML expertise.

options.text: Amazon EC2 with self-managed TensorFlow

explanation.summary: Self-managed TensorFlow requires significant ML and infrastructure management skills.
explanation.why: Running TensorFlow on EC2 involves manual environment setup, model engineering, infrastructure scaling, and operational maintenance, which conflicts with the low-code requirement.

questions.question: Engineers across teams keep recomputing the same features (rolling averages, customer lifetime value, recency scores), causing duplicate work and inconsistent definitions. The lead wants a managed repository where features are defined once and reused for training and real-time inference. Which fits?

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB tables with custom application logic

explanation.summary: DynamoDB alone does not provide centralized feature lifecycle management.
explanation.why: Although DynamoDB can store feature values, teams would still need to build custom pipelines, governance, feature definitions, and synchronization logic manually.

options.text: Amazon S3 with manual folder organization

explanation.summary: Manual storage organization lacks dedicated feature serving and governance capabilities.
explanation.why: S3 provides scalable object storage but does not manage reusable ML features, online serving, feature lineage, or centralized feature consistency.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Feature Store for centralized feature management

explanation.summary: SageMaker Feature Store centralizes reusable ML feature definitions and serving.
explanation.why: Amazon SageMaker Feature Store allows teams to define features once, reuse them across models, and support both training and real-time inference workloads. It improves consistency, reduces duplicated feature engineering, and supports online and offline feature access.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Registry

explanation.summary: Model Registry manages trained model versions rather than reusable features.
explanation.why: SageMaker Model Registry is designed for model governance, versioning, and deployment tracking, not centralized feature storage and reuse.
explanation.comparison: Feature Store manages features, while Model Registry manages models.

questions.question: A media company is exploring generative AI for content creation. The team needs to understand the fundamental mechanism by which generative AI models produce new outputs not present in training data, such as original text, images, and music. Which choice best describes this mechanism?

options.text: By using pre-defined rules and templates without any learning from data

explanation.summary: Rule-based systems do not learn statistical patterns from large datasets.
explanation.why: Generative AI relies on machine learning and statistical pattern learning rather than hardcoded templates and deterministic rules.

options.text: Through traditional programming methods where each outcome is manually coded

explanation.summary: Traditional programming manually defines logic instead of learning from data.
explanation.why: Generative AI models automatically learn representations and patterns from training datasets rather than relying entirely on developer-written instructions.

options.text: By randomly assembling content from a library of existing data with no learned structure

explanation.summary: Generative AI produces structured outputs using learned representations rather than random assembly.
explanation.why: Generative models learn statistical relationships and semantic structure from training data. Outputs are generated probabilistically, not by random copy-pasting from stored examples.

options.text: By learning statistical patterns from training data and using those patterns to generate new content that resembles but does not copy the originals

explanation.summary: Generative AI creates new outputs by modeling statistical patterns learned from large datasets.
explanation.why: Generative models learn probability distributions, semantic relationships, and latent representations from training data. They use these learned patterns to generate novel text, images, audio, or code that resembles the training data without directly reproducing exact originals.

questions.question: A technology officer is briefing executives on the relationship between several AI terms they have been hearing: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and Generative AI. The officer needs to explain how these concepts relate to each other in terms of scope and inclusion.

options.text: All four terms refer to the same thing and are interchangeable

explanation.summary: These AI concepts represent different scopes and specialized subfields.
explanation.why: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and Generative AI are related but distinct concepts with hierarchical relationships rather than interchangeable meanings.

options.text: Generative AI is the broadest term and contains AI, ML, and Deep Learning as subsets

explanation.summary: Generative AI is a specialized subset rather than the broadest AI category.
explanation.why: Generative AI is built on deep learning techniques and therefore exists within the broader AI hierarchy instead of containing it.

options.text: AI is the broadest field; ML is a subset of AI; Deep Learning is a subset of ML; Generative AI is a subset of Deep Learning

explanation.summary: AI concepts form a nested hierarchy from broad intelligence systems to specialized generative models.
explanation.why: Artificial Intelligence is the broadest discipline encompassing systems that mimic intelligent behavior. Machine Learning is a subset focused on learning from data. Deep Learning is a specialized ML approach using neural networks, and Generative AI commonly relies on deep learning models to generate new content.
keyPoints: Generative AI builds on deep learning
explanation.comparison: Each category becomes more specialized moving downward in the hierarchy.

learnMore.title: AI vs ML vs Deep Learning

options.text: The four terms are completely independent fields with no overlap

explanation.summary: These technologies overlap heavily and are hierarchically related.
explanation.why: Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and Generative AI are all specialized branches within the broader AI ecosystem rather than isolated disciplines.

questions.question: A product manager is evaluating Amazon Bedrock for an internal AI assistant. Which two techniques are commonly used in enterprise AI assistant workflows that combine an organization's proprietary documents with the reasoning ability of a foundation model? (Select two)

options.text: Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)

explanation.summary: GANs are primarily used for synthetic data and image generation tasks.
explanation.why: Generative Adversarial Networks are specialized architectures commonly used for image synthesis, style transfer, and synthetic data generation. They are not the standard architecture for enterprise document-grounded AI assistants.

options.text: Large Language Model (LLM)

explanation.summary: LLMs provide the reasoning and language generation engine for AI assistants.
explanation.why: Enterprise AI assistants commonly rely on Large Language Models to perform reasoning, summarization, question answering, conversational interaction, and text generation tasks across many domains.

options.text: Variational Autoencoder (VAE)

explanation.summary: VAEs are generative modeling architectures rather than enterprise assistant retrieval workflows.
explanation.why: Variational Autoencoders are used for representation learning and generative modeling tasks but are not commonly used as the primary architecture for enterprise document-grounded assistants.

options.text: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

explanation.summary: RAG combines proprietary enterprise documents with foundation model reasoning at query time.
explanation.why: Retrieval-Augmented Generation retrieves relevant organizational documents from a knowledge base and injects them into the model context before generation. This grounds responses in trusted enterprise information while leveraging the reasoning capabilities of the LLM.
explanation.comparison: RAG dynamically retrieves knowledge, while fine-tuning embeds behavior into model weights.

questions.question: A customer service team is testing a generative AI chatbot. During testing, it occasionally produces confident-sounding answers containing fabricated facts, including invented product features and made-up policies. What is the technical name for this phenomenon, and what causes it?

options.text: Bias, caused by skewed training data

explanation.summary: Bias refers to unfair or skewed behavior learned from datasets.
explanation.why: Bias involves systematic unfairness or unequal treatment caused by imbalanced or problematic training data. The question specifically describes fabricated information rather than discriminatory outputs.

options.text: Drift, caused by changes in real-world data over time

explanation.summary: Data drift refers to changing production data distributions after deployment.
explanation.why: Drift affects prediction quality as real-world inputs evolve over time, but it does not specifically describe fabricated generative outputs.

options.text: Overfitting, caused by memorizing training examples

explanation.summary: Overfitting occurs when a model memorizes training data too closely.
explanation.why: Overfitting causes weak generalization performance but does not directly explain confident fabrication of nonexistent facts during generation.

options.text: Hallucination, caused by the model generating plausible-sounding but factually incorrect content

explanation.summary: Hallucinations occur when generative models produce realistic but incorrect information.
explanation.why: Large language models generate text probabilistically based on learned statistical patterns rather than true factual understanding. When grounding information is insufficient or context is ambiguous, the model may produce fabricated but convincing responses.

questions.question: A team is comparing Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Fine-Tuning. Their data is a constantly changing internal knowledge base with thousands of policy documents updated weekly. Which approach is more appropriate for grounding the model in this knowledge?

options.text: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, because it grounds responses in current documents at query time without retraining

explanation.summary: RAG dynamically retrieves current knowledge without requiring repeated retraining.
explanation.why: Retrieval-Augmented Generation retrieves relevant documents at query time and provides them to the model as context. This makes it ideal for rapidly changing knowledge bases where policies and documents are updated frequently.
explanation.comparison: RAG retrieves live knowledge, while fine-tuning embeds static knowledge into weights.

options.text: Fine-Tuning, because it permanently embeds the knowledge into model weights

explanation.summary: Fine-tuning is less suitable for rapidly changing knowledge bases.
explanation.why: Fine-tuning modifies model weights using training examples and works best for persistent behaviors or style adaptation. Frequently updated policy documents would require repeated retraining cycles, increasing operational overhead.

options.text: Pretraining a new foundation model from scratch on the policy documents

explanation.summary: Training a foundation model from scratch is unnecessary and extremely resource intensive.
explanation.why: Pretraining foundation models requires enormous datasets, compute resources, and engineering complexity. Enterprise policy grounding is typically solved using RAG architectures instead.

options.text: Few-shot prompting with all policy documents in the prompt every time

explanation.summary: Including all documents in prompts is inefficient and limited by context windows.
explanation.why: Large policy repositories quickly exceed model context limits and become operationally inefficient. Retrieval systems selectively provide only the most relevant documents.

questions.question: A data science team is configuring inference parameters on Amazon Bedrock for a legal summary generator. They want responses that are more deterministic and focused, reducing creative variation, since consistency and accuracy matter more than creativity. Which parameter adjustment best fits?

options.text: Increase temperature toward 1.0 for more diverse outputs

explanation.summary: Higher temperature increases randomness and creativity in generated responses.
explanation.why: Raising the temperature parameter causes the model to sample from a wider range of possible tokens, producing more varied and creative outputs rather than deterministic responses.

options.text: Lower temperature toward 0.0 for more deterministic outputs

explanation.summary: Lower temperature reduces randomness and produces more consistent responses.
explanation.why: Temperature controls token sampling randomness during generation. Lowering temperature toward 0.0 makes outputs more deterministic, focused, and repeatable, which is ideal for legal summaries and enterprise compliance scenarios.

options.text: Increase Top P to near 1.0 to consider all candidate tokens

explanation.summary: Higher Top P generally increases diversity by expanding candidate token selection.
explanation.why: Top P controls nucleus sampling by selecting from the most probable tokens until a probability threshold is reached. Increasing it broadly allows more candidate choices and may increase variability.

options.text: Increase max tokens to allow longer responses

explanation.summary: Max tokens controls output length rather than determinism.
explanation.why: Increasing maximum token count allows the model to generate longer responses but does not directly affect consistency, randomness, or creativity.

questions.question: A research team is comparing prompt engineering techniques for a foundation model that must solve multi-step math word problems. They want the model to show its reasoning explicitly, breaking each problem into logical intermediate steps before the final answer. Which technique should they use?

options.text: Zero-shot prompting with no examples

explanation.summary: Zero-shot prompting does not explicitly encourage intermediate reasoning steps.
explanation.why: While zero-shot prompts can sometimes solve simple tasks, they do not inherently guide the model through structured step-by-step reasoning.

options.text: Increasing max tokens to a high value

explanation.summary: Allowing longer outputs does not automatically produce logical reasoning chains.
explanation.why: Max token limits only affect potential response length and do not guarantee structured intermediate reasoning.

options.text: Temperature reduction to zero

explanation.summary: Lower temperature improves determinism but not explicit reasoning structure.
explanation.why: Reducing temperature makes outputs more predictable but does not specifically encourage the model to explain intermediate reasoning steps.

options.text: Chain-of-thought prompting to encourage step-by-step reasoning

explanation.summary: Chain-of-thought prompting guides models to reason through intermediate logical steps.
explanation.why: Chain-of-thought prompting encourages the model to decompose complex problems into sequential reasoning steps before producing a final answer. This improves performance on multi-step reasoning and mathematical problem-solving tasks.

questions.question: A product architect is documenting the defining characteristics of foundation models for a generative AI workshop. Which two statements accurately describe foundation models? (Select two)

options.text: They are trained on broad, diverse data at large scale

explanation.summary: Foundation models learn generalized representations from massive and diverse datasets.
explanation.why: Foundation models are pretrained on extremely large datasets containing text, images, code, audio, and other modalities. This broad training enables them to generalize across many downstream tasks rather than being limited to one narrow application.

options.text: They are designed for a single narrow task only

explanation.summary: Foundation models are general-purpose rather than single-task systems.
explanation.why: Unlike traditional ML models trained specifically for one problem, foundation models can adapt to many downstream tasks using prompting, RAG, or fine-tuning.
explanation.comparison: Traditional ML often targets one task, while foundation models support many tasks.

options.text: They can be adapted to many downstream tasks through prompting, RAG, or fine-tuning

explanation.summary: Foundation models are reusable across many applications through adaptation techniques.
explanation.why: After pretraining, foundation models can perform tasks such as summarization, classification, chat, and code generation using prompting, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, or fine-tuning without retraining a completely new model from scratch.

options.text: They require labeled training data for every new use case

explanation.summary: Foundation models reduce dependence on task-specific labeled datasets.
explanation.why: Foundation models already contain broad pretrained knowledge and can often solve tasks using prompting alone, without requiring large labeled datasets for every new application.

questions.question: An enterprise architecture team needs a managed AWS service providing access to powerful foundation models for multilingual summarization, question answering, and reasoning over long documents. They do not want to host models themselves or build custom infrastructure. Which AWS service best satisfies this requirement?

options.text: Train a custom model from scratch using Amazon SageMaker

explanation.summary: Training custom foundation models from scratch is complex and resource intensive.
explanation.why: Building and training large foundation models requires massive datasets, specialized expertise, GPU infrastructure, and high operational costs, which contradicts the requirement for a managed solution.

options.text: Deploy an open-source LLM manually on Amazon EC2

explanation.summary: Self-hosting LLMs requires infrastructure management and operational overhead.
explanation.why: Managing models on EC2 involves scaling, patching, GPU provisioning, monitoring, and deployment complexity, which the organization explicitly wants to avoid.

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock to access a foundation model that meets the criteria through a managed API

explanation.summary: Amazon Bedrock provides managed access to foundation models through APIs.
explanation.why: Amazon Bedrock enables organizations to use powerful foundation models for tasks such as summarization, question answering, multilingual reasoning, and document analysis without managing infrastructure or hosting models themselves.

options.text: Use Amazon Comprehend for all summarization and reasoning tasks

explanation.summary: Comprehend is designed for NLP analysis rather than advanced generative reasoning.
explanation.why: Amazon Comprehend performs tasks such as sentiment analysis and entity extraction, but it is not a foundation model platform supporting advanced generative AI reasoning and long-context summarization.
explanation.comparison: Comprehend analyzes text, while Bedrock provides generative foundation models.

questions.question: A marketing company has collected 5,000 high-quality examples of its desired brand voice and writing style. The goal is to make future generations consistently match this tone with minimal prompting overhead. Which adaptation strategy is most appropriate?

options.text: Zero-shot prompting with no examples

explanation.summary: Zero-shot prompting provides no persistent guidance for a specialized writing style.
explanation.why: Without examples or adaptation, the model may generate inconsistent tone and style across requests because the desired brand voice is not embedded into model behavior.

options.text: Few-shot prompting with three examples in every prompt

explanation.summary: Few-shot prompting provides temporary guidance but increases prompt overhead.
explanation.why: Few-shot examples can improve style consistency, but repeating examples in every request consumes context space and does not permanently internalize the brand voice.
explanation.comparison: Few-shot prompting guides behavior temporarily, while fine-tuning embeds patterns into model weights.

options.text: Fine-tuning the model on the 5,000 examples to embed the voice in model weights

explanation.summary: Fine-tuning adapts model behavior to consistently reflect a desired writing style.
explanation.why: Fine-tuning trains the model on high-quality examples so the desired tone, phrasing, and stylistic patterns become embedded into the model weights. This reduces prompt complexity and improves long-term consistency across generations.

options.text: Retrieval-Augmented Generation against the 5,000 writing examples

explanation.summary: RAG is primarily used for grounding factual knowledge rather than persistent style learning.
explanation.why: Retrieval-Augmented Generation retrieves reference content dynamically, which is useful for factual grounding and knowledge access. The requirement here is consistent stylistic behavior across outputs rather than knowledge retrieval.

questions.question: A startup wants a fully managed enterprise AI assistant that answers employee questions from internal documents in Microsoft 365, Confluence, ServiceNow, and Salesforce. They prefer an out-of-the-box solution with built-in connectors rather than a custom RAG pipeline. Which AWS service fits?

options.text: Amazon Q Business for fully managed enterprise AI assistance

explanation.summary: Amazon Q Business provides a managed enterprise AI assistant with built-in enterprise connectors.
explanation.why: Amazon Q Business is designed specifically for enterprise generative AI use cases. It supports built-in integrations with systems such as Microsoft 365, Confluence, ServiceNow, and Salesforce, enabling organizations to deploy AI-powered assistants without building custom retrieval pipelines or infrastructure.
explanation.comparison: Amazon Q Business provides turnkey enterprise AI assistance, while Bedrock is a lower-level foundation model platform.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock with custom RAG pipeline using Knowledge Bases

explanation.summary: Bedrock Knowledge Bases still requires designing and managing a custom AI workflow.
explanation.why: Although Amazon Bedrock supports Retrieval-Augmented Generation through Knowledge Bases, the scenario specifically requests a fully managed out-of-the-box assistant with enterprise connectors rather than a custom implementation.
explanation.comparison: Bedrock offers building blocks, while Amazon Q Business provides a ready-made enterprise assistant.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart with a pretrained LLM

explanation.summary: JumpStart helps deploy models but is not a turnkey enterprise assistant platform.
explanation.why: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart provides pretrained models and ML templates, but organizations would still need to build retrieval, connectors, orchestration, and enterprise search functionality themselves.

options.text: Amazon Lex for chatbot development

explanation.summary: Amazon Lex focuses on conversational chatbot interfaces rather than enterprise document intelligence.
explanation.why: Amazon Lex is designed for intent-based conversational bots and voice/text interfaces. It does not provide the enterprise generative AI retrieval and connector ecosystem described in the scenario.

questions.question: A user is constructing a prompt for a foundation model. The user wants to understand the conventional components of a well-structured prompt that consistently produces high-quality output. Which three components are standard parts of a well-designed prompt? (Select three)

options.text: Clear instructions describing the task

explanation.summary: Instructions define the task and expected behavior for the model.
explanation.why: Clear instructions tell the foundation model exactly what task to perform, the desired output style, formatting expectations, constraints, and objectives. Well-written instructions improve consistency and output quality.

options.text: Context or background information relevant to the task

explanation.summary: Context provides supporting information that helps the model generate better responses.
explanation.why: Including relevant context gives the model additional grounding information, constraints, or domain-specific details that improve relevance and accuracy of outputs.

options.text: Examples demonstrating desired output (few-shot)

explanation.summary: Few-shot examples demonstrate the desired structure, style, or reasoning pattern.
explanation.why: Providing examples helps the model infer formatting, reasoning style, tone, and expected output structure, improving consistency and task performance.

options.text: The model's internal weights

explanation.summary: Model weights are part of the pretrained model architecture rather than user-controlled prompt components.
explanation.why: Internal weights are learned parameters stored within the foundation model during training. Users cannot directly include or modify them as part of prompt construction.
explanation.comparison: Prompts are external instructions, while model weights are internal learned parameters.

questions.question: A team is evaluating the tradeoffs between several foundation model adaptation approaches: prompt engineering, RAG, fine-tuning, and continued pretraining. They want to understand the COST and EFFORT ordering of these approaches from lowest to highest.

options.text: Continued pretraining < Fine-tuning < RAG < Prompt engineering

explanation.summary: Continued pretraining is typically the most expensive and operationally complex adaptation method.
explanation.why: Continued pretraining requires massive datasets, specialized compute infrastructure, and large-scale training operations. Prompt engineering is usually the least expensive because it modifies prompts rather than retraining models.
explanation.comparison: The actual progression moves from lightweight prompting toward increasingly expensive model training approaches.

options.text: RAG < Continued pretraining < Prompt engineering < Fine-tuning

explanation.summary: Prompt engineering is generally lower cost and effort than RAG or model retraining methods.
explanation.why: RAG requires retrieval infrastructure such as embeddings, vector databases, and orchestration layers, while prompt engineering can often be implemented immediately without additional infrastructure.

options.text: Fine-tuning < Prompt engineering < Continued pretraining < RAG

explanation.summary: Fine-tuning requires more compute, data, and operational effort than prompt engineering.
explanation.why: Fine-tuning modifies model weights using training jobs and curated datasets, making it more resource intensive than prompt engineering or many RAG implementations.

options.text: Prompt engineering < RAG < Fine-tuning < Continued pretraining

explanation.summary: Foundation model adaptation methods increase in cost and complexity from prompting to large-scale retraining.
explanation.why: Prompt engineering is the simplest and lowest-cost approach because it changes only instructions. RAG adds retrieval pipelines and vector search infrastructure. Fine-tuning introduces supervised training and model adaptation. Continued pretraining is the most expensive because it requires large-scale compute, datasets, and extended training similar to building foundation models.

questions.question: A health technology startup is evaluating embedding models for a semantic search application over a corpus of clinical research papers. The team needs to understand what an embedding is and how it enables semantic search.

options.text: An embedding is a compressed image of the text; semantic search compares pixel similarity

explanation.summary: Embeddings are numeric semantic representations rather than image compressions.
explanation.why: Semantic embeddings represent textual meaning mathematically in vector space. Semantic search compares vector similarity, not image pixels.

options.text: An embedding is a keyword index; semantic search performs exact keyword matching

explanation.summary: Semantic search focuses on meaning rather than exact keyword matching.
explanation.why: Traditional lexical search relies on keyword overlap, while embeddings allow retrieval based on conceptual similarity and semantic relationships.
explanation.comparison: Keyword search matches words directly, while semantic search matches meaning.

options.text: An embedding is a numeric vector that represents the meaning of text; semantic search compares vectors using distance metrics like cosine similarity

explanation.summary: Embeddings encode semantic meaning as numeric vectors for similarity comparison.
explanation.why: Embedding models transform text into high-dimensional numeric vectors that capture semantic relationships. Semantic search converts both documents and user queries into embeddings, then compares them using similarity metrics such as cosine similarity to retrieve meaningfully related content.
explanation.comparison: Semantic search retrieves conceptually related content even when exact keywords differ.

options.text: An embedding is the raw bytes of the text file; semantic search uses substring matching

explanation.summary: Embeddings are learned semantic representations rather than raw file bytes.
explanation.why: Raw bytes and substring matching do not capture contextual or conceptual meaning. Embeddings use learned representations from neural models to encode semantics.

questions.question: A small business owner is exploring AWS generative AI services and notices three different ways to interact with foundation models: through Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Q, and PartyRock. The owner wants to understand the primary purpose and target audience of each.

options.text: All three are the same product with different names

explanation.summary: Bedrock, Amazon Q, and PartyRock serve different audiences and use cases.
explanation.why: These AWS offerings target different layers of the generative AI ecosystem. They are complementary services rather than identical products with renamed branding.

options.text: Bedrock is for developers building applications with foundation models; Amazon Q is a managed AI assistant for end users; PartyRock is a free playground for learning and prototyping

explanation.summary: AWS provides different generative AI offerings for developers, enterprise users, and experimentation.
explanation.why: Amazon Bedrock is a developer platform for building generative AI applications using foundation models through APIs. Amazon Q is an end-user focused AI assistant for enterprise productivity and business workflows. PartyRock is a lightweight educational and prototyping environment designed for experimentation and learning without deep AWS expertise.
explanation.comparison: Bedrock provides foundational AI infrastructure, while Amazon Q provides ready-to-use AI assistance.

options.text: Bedrock is for end users, Q is for developers, PartyRock is for enterprises

explanation.summary: This option reverses the primary intended audiences of the AWS services.
explanation.why: Amazon Bedrock is developer-oriented infrastructure for building AI applications, while Amazon Q is the enterprise-facing managed assistant solution.

options.text: Q and PartyRock are deprecated, only Bedrock remains

explanation.summary: Amazon Q and PartyRock remain active AWS generative AI offerings.
explanation.why: AWS continues to support and expand Amazon Q and PartyRock alongside Bedrock as part of its broader generative AI portfolio.

questions.question: A team is implementing RAG with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases over a corpus of 50,000 PDF documents. The team needs to understand why documents must be chunked before embeddings are created, rather than embedding entire documents as single units.

options.text: Chunking reduces storage costs by compressing the text

explanation.summary: Chunking is primarily about retrieval granularity rather than compression.
explanation.why: Document chunking improves retrieval precision and context management in RAG systems, but it is not a text compression technique intended to minimize storage costs.

options.text: Chunking randomizes the document order to improve security

explanation.summary: Chunking is unrelated to document randomization or security enhancement.
explanation.why: The purpose of chunking is to create semantically meaningful text segments that improve embedding quality and retrieval precision, not to provide security controls.

options.text: Chunking is required by AWS for legal compliance

explanation.summary: Chunking is a technical retrieval optimization strategy rather than a compliance requirement.
explanation.why: AWS does not mandate chunking for legal compliance. Chunking is used because large documents reduce embedding and retrieval effectiveness when treated as single vectors.

options.text: Chunking divides documents into smaller pieces that fit within context windows and improve retrieval precision

explanation.summary: Chunking improves semantic retrieval quality and enables efficient use of model context windows.
explanation.why: RAG systems work best when documents are divided into smaller semantic sections before embedding generation. Smaller chunks improve vector similarity matching, reduce irrelevant retrieved content, fit within model context limits, and allow more precise grounding during question answering.
explanation.comparison: Embedding entire documents often dilutes semantic meaning and retrieves large amounts of irrelevant information.

questions.question: A developer building a Bedrock chatbot is concerned about attacks where users craft inputs designed to make the model ignore system instructions, leak its system prompt, or bypass safety filters. What is the technical name for this attack class, and what is the primary defense available on Bedrock?

options.text: SQL injection, defended by parameterized queries

explanation.summary: SQL injection targets database query execution rather than foundation model prompts.
explanation.why: SQL injection attacks manipulate database queries through unsanitized inputs. The scenario instead describes adversarial manipulation of model instructions and prompt behavior, which is a generative AI security concern rather than a database vulnerability.
explanation.comparison: SQL injection targets databases, while prompt injection targets foundation model behavior.

options.text: Prompt injection, defended by Bedrock Guardrails prompt attack filters and input validation

explanation.summary: Prompt injection attacks attempt to manipulate model instructions and bypass safety controls.
explanation.why: Prompt injection occurs when malicious or crafted user inputs attempt to override system prompts, expose hidden instructions, bypass policies, or manipulate model behavior. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails provides protections such as prompt attack filtering, harmful content controls, denied topics, and input validation to help mitigate these attacks.
explanation.comparison: Prompt injection affects LLM reasoning and behavior rather than backend databases or browsers.

options.text: Cross-site scripting, defended by content security policies

explanation.summary: Cross-site scripting targets browser-based applications rather than foundation model prompts.
explanation.why: Cross-site scripting injects malicious scripts into web applications viewed by browsers. The scenario describes manipulation of AI model instructions rather than browser execution.

options.text: Denial of service, defended by rate limiting alone

explanation.summary: Denial of service attacks focus on resource exhaustion rather than instruction manipulation.
explanation.why: The scenario involves adversarial prompts attempting to manipulate AI behavior and system instructions, which differs from overwhelming systems with excessive traffic or requests.

questions.question: A healthcare company is deploying a Bedrock patient chatbot. Compliance requires that patient identifiers like names, Social Security numbers, addresses, and medical record numbers be automatically detected and masked in both inputs and outputs. Which Bedrock Guardrails feature handles this?

options.text: Content filters for harmful content categories

explanation.summary: Content filters focus on harmful or unsafe language categories rather than PII masking.
explanation.why: Content filters are designed to detect categories such as hate speech, violence, harassment, or toxic content. They do not specifically identify and redact sensitive personal identifiers.

options.text: Denied topics for restricting subject areas

explanation.summary: Denied topics restrict conversational subject matter rather than detecting personal identifiers.
explanation.why: Denied topics are used to block or restrict discussions about specified domains or subjects, not to identify and mask sensitive information such as SSNs or medical record identifiers.

options.text: Sensitive information filters with PII detection and masking

explanation.summary: Sensitive information filters detect and redact personally identifiable information in prompts and responses.
explanation.why: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails includes sensitive information filters that can automatically identify and mask personally identifiable information (PII) such as names, addresses, Social Security numbers, phone numbers, and medical identifiers in both model inputs and outputs.
explanation.comparison: Sensitive information filters target privacy protection, while content filters target harmful content moderation.

learnMore.title: Sensitive Information Filters in Bedrock Guardrails

options.text: Contextual grounding checks for hallucination detection

explanation.summary: Grounding checks compare model responses against source documents to reduce hallucinations.
explanation.why: Contextual grounding helps determine whether generated responses are supported by trusted reference content, but it does not specifically detect or redact personally identifiable information.

questions.question: A data analyst is evaluating model output quality for a SUMMARIZATION task. The analyst needs a metric specifically designed to measure how well generated summaries overlap with reference summaries written by humans. Which metric is the standard choice?

options.text: Perplexity, which measures how well the model predicts text

explanation.summary: Perplexity evaluates language modeling quality rather than summary overlap accuracy.
explanation.why: Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token in text sequences. It is commonly used for evaluating language models themselves, not for comparing generated summaries against human references.
explanation.comparison: Perplexity evaluates prediction confidence, while ROUGE evaluates overlap with reference summaries.

options.text: ROUGE, which measures overlap between generated and reference summaries

explanation.summary: ROUGE is the standard summarization metric for comparing generated summaries against human references.
explanation.why: ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation) measures overlap between generated summaries and reference summaries using metrics such as n-gram overlap, longest common subsequences, and recall-oriented matching. It is widely used in summarization benchmarks and research.
keyPoints: Supports ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L variants
explanation.comparison: ROUGE focuses on summary similarity, while BLEU was originally designed for translation tasks.

options.text: Accuracy, which measures categorical correctness

explanation.summary: Accuracy is primarily used for classification tasks with discrete labels.
explanation.why: Summarization outputs are open-ended text generations rather than fixed categorical predictions, making accuracy unsuitable for evaluating summary quality.

options.text: BLEU, which was designed for translation evaluation

explanation.summary: BLEU was primarily created for machine translation evaluation rather than summarization.
explanation.why: BLEU measures overlap precision between generated and reference translations. While it can sometimes be applied to other text generation tasks, ROUGE is the standard metric for summarization.
explanation.comparison: BLEU is translation-focused, while ROUGE is summary-focused.

questions.question: A team is using Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to power a customer support assistant. The team wants to evaluate which combination of components is required to build a working RAG application on AWS. Which three components are required? (Select three)

options.text: An embedding model to convert text into vectors

explanation.summary: Embedding models convert text into semantic vector representations for retrieval.
explanation.why: RAG systems rely on embeddings to encode documents and user queries into vector space so semantically similar content can be retrieved efficiently.

options.text: A vector store to index and search the embeddings

explanation.summary: Vector databases store embeddings and perform semantic similarity search.
explanation.why: A vector store indexes embedding vectors and retrieves the most semantically relevant chunks using nearest-neighbor search techniques.

options.text: A generative foundation model to produce final responses

explanation.summary: Foundation models generate grounded responses using retrieved context.
explanation.why: After relevant context is retrieved from the vector store, a foundation model synthesizes the information and generates the final natural-language response.

options.text: A separate fine-tuned model for each customer

explanation.summary: RAG systems do not require customer-specific fine-tuned models.
explanation.why: RAG dynamically retrieves external knowledge at query time, allowing a shared foundation model to answer questions without retraining or maintaining separate models per customer.
explanation.comparison: RAG grounds responses through retrieval rather than customer-specific retraining.

questions.question: A team is using Amazon SageMaker for production deployment. The workload has very large payloads (up to 1 GB per request) and long processing times (up to one hour), but can tolerate near-real-time latency rather than instant response. Which SageMaker inference option fits this profile?

options.text: Asynchronous inference for large payloads and long processing times

explanation.summary: Asynchronous inference supports large payloads and long-running inference jobs.
explanation.why: Amazon SageMaker Asynchronous Inference is designed for requests with large payloads and long processing durations. It queues requests, processes them asynchronously, and returns results later through storage destinations such as Amazon S3.

options.text: Serverless inference for sporadic workloads

explanation.summary: Serverless inference is optimized for lightweight intermittent workloads rather than large long-running jobs.
explanation.why: Serverless inference is intended for variable or infrequent traffic patterns with moderate payload sizes and relatively fast responses.

options.text: Real-time inference with always-on endpoints

explanation.summary: Real-time endpoints are designed for low-latency interactive inference workloads.
explanation.why: Real-time inference is optimized for fast response times rather than large payloads and long processing durations.

options.text: Batch transform for offline scoring

explanation.summary: Batch transform is designed for offline dataset processing rather than asynchronous request-response workflows.
explanation.why: Batch transform processes entire datasets stored in locations such as Amazon S3 rather than handling queued asynchronous API requests.

questions.question: A startup wants to prototype quickly with a pretrained foundation model. They want a curated catalog of pretrained models from AWS, Hugging Face, and other providers, deployable with a single click and customizable via fine-tuning. Which AWS feature matches this need?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth for data labeling

explanation.summary: Ground Truth focuses on data labeling workflows rather than pretrained model deployment.
explanation.why: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth is designed for creating labeled datasets for machine learning training and annotation tasks.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Pipelines for ML workflow orchestration

explanation.summary: SageMaker Pipelines orchestrates ML workflows but is not a pretrained model catalog.
explanation.why: Pipelines helps automate ML CI/CD workflows and model lifecycle processes rather than providing one-click pretrained foundation model deployment.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart for pretrained models and solutions

explanation.summary: SageMaker JumpStart provides curated pretrained models with rapid deployment and fine-tuning support.
explanation.why: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart offers a catalog of pretrained models and ML solutions from AWS, Hugging Face, and third-party providers. Teams can deploy models with one click and customize them through fine-tuning workflows.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Clarify for bias detection

explanation.summary: SageMaker Clarify focuses on bias detection and explainability rather than pretrained model catalogs.
explanation.why: Clarify helps detect bias and explain model predictions, but it does not provide rapid pretrained model deployment.

questions.question: A development team is comparing Amazon Bedrock Agents and AWS Step Functions for orchestrating a workflow that involves multiple AWS service calls. The team needs to understand the key difference between these two services. Which statement best describes the difference?

options.text: Bedrock Agents and Step Functions are the same service with different names

explanation.summary: Bedrock Agents and Step Functions solve different orchestration problems.
explanation.why: AWS Step Functions provides deterministic workflow orchestration, while Bedrock Agents add foundation-model-driven reasoning and dynamic decision-making.

options.text: Step Functions only works with Lambda; Bedrock Agents only works with Bedrock

explanation.summary: Both services integrate broadly across AWS services and external APIs.
explanation.why: AWS Step Functions supports many AWS integrations beyond Lambda, and Bedrock Agents can orchestrate external APIs and tools through action groups.

options.text: Bedrock Agents use a foundation model to dynamically reason about which steps to take; Step Functions executes a predefined workflow defined in advance

explanation.summary: Bedrock Agents provide AI-driven dynamic orchestration while Step Functions executes deterministic workflows.
explanation.why: Amazon Bedrock Agents use foundation models to interpret requests, reason about goals, and dynamically decide which tools or APIs to invoke. AWS Step Functions executes explicitly defined state-machine workflows where every branch and step is predetermined.
explanation.comparison: Bedrock Agents emphasize adaptive AI orchestration, while Step Functions emphasize predictable automation.

options.text: Bedrock Agents are deprecated; Step Functions is the replacement

explanation.summary: Bedrock Agents is an active AWS generative AI capability.
explanation.why: Amazon Bedrock Agents continues to be actively supported and expanded by AWS for generative AI orchestration workloads.

questions.question: A team building an internal Bedrock application wants to systematically compare two candidate foundation models on the same prompts and reference answers. They need a managed AWS feature that runs automated and human evaluation workflows against benchmarks. Which feature is most appropriate?

options.text: AWS X-Ray for distributed tracing

explanation.summary: AWS X-Ray is designed for tracing distributed applications rather than evaluating model quality.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor for production drift detection

explanation.why: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor detects changes in production data and model quality over time, but it is not intended for benchmark-based generative AI evaluation workflows.

options.text: Amazon CloudWatch dashboards for operational metrics

explanation.summary: CloudWatch dashboards provide operational observability rather than model benchmarking.
explanation.why: Amazon CloudWatch monitors infrastructure and application metrics, not generative AI response quality comparisons.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation for automated and human evaluation

explanation.summary: Bedrock Model Evaluation supports benchmark-driven automated and human assessment of foundation models.
explanation.why: Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation enables side-by-side comparisons of candidate foundation models using standardized prompts, reference answers, automated scoring metrics, and human evaluation workflows.

questions.question: A company using Amazon SageMaker wants to streamline the work of data scientists who currently write code in different IDEs. The team is exploring SageMaker Studio's integrated development environments to standardize workflow. Which IDEs are available within SageMaker Studio? (Select all that apply)

options.text: RStudio

questions.question: A team needs to label 200,000 images with bounding boxes around vehicles for an object detection model. They want a managed AWS service supporting human labelers (in-house, AWS-managed Mechanical Turk, or third-party vendors) with automatic labeling assistance to reduce cost. Which service fits?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth for managed data labeling

explanation.why: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth is designed for large-scale supervised labeling workflows including bounding boxes for object detection datasets. options.text: Amazon Mechanical Turk alone with no automation

options.text: Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels for the entire workflow

questions.question: A multinational company is building a customer experience platform and needs multilingual support so users can interact in their preferred language. options.text: Amazon Transcribe for translation between languages

options.text: Amazon Polly for translation

options.text: Amazon Rekognition for language tasks

options.text: Amazon Translate for real-time text translation, with built-in or Comprehend-based language detection

explanation.summary: Neural machine translation supports multilingual communication and language detection.

questions.question: A team is designing an architecture for a generative AI assistant. Option A connects the foundation model directly to enterprise APIs through tool use. Option B retrieves enterprise document chunks and inserts them into the prompt at query time. Which pattern correctly maps to which use case?

options.text: Both patterns are the same and interchangeable for any use case

explanation.summary: Tool use and retrieval augmentation solve different architectural problems.
explanation.why: Tool use enables external actions and API orchestration, while RAG retrieves contextual information from document stores for grounded responses.
explanation.comparison: Tool use focuses on actions; RAG focuses on knowledge retrieval.

options.text: Neither pattern is suitable for production use

explanation.summary: Both RAG and tool use are standard enterprise generative AI patterns.
explanation.why: Modern enterprise AI assistants commonly combine API orchestration and retrieval augmentation for production applications.

options.text: Option A is best for document Q&A; Option B is best for API calls

explanation.why: Option A describes tool use and action orchestration through APIs, while Option B describes retrieval-augmented generation using document chunks.

options.text: Option A is best for tasks requiring real-time actions (booking, updating records); Option B is best for tasks requiring information lookup from documents

questions.question: A team needs to extract structured data from invoices, receipts, and forms in image and PDF format. The data includes both text and tabular content like line items. Which AWS service provides specialized capabilities for document text and form extraction with structure preservation?

options.text: Amazon Textract for document text, tables, and forms extraction
